newsitem.title: GERMANY: F.O. LICHT - Daily coffee report.
newsitem.headline: F.O. LICHT - Daily coffee report.

text.p: The following is a direct contribution from statistician F.O. Licht in Ratzeburg, Germany. Please address any queries to Helmut Ahlfeld on +00 49 4541 88920.

Robusta futures in London ended a choppy session weaker after a slide in New York arabica futures sparked losses in London. November closed $7 lower at $1,545 a tonne while September was down $13 at $1,595 a tonne. September's premium to November narrowed to $50 a tonne by the close as gradings increased. In New York arabica futures ended sharply lower, battered by waning supply concerns and news of impending reduction to speculative position limits on the Exchange's 'C' coffee contract. However, some traders said that the latter argument is an excuse due to a lack of other concrete news to explain the fall in coffee prices. It was added that in reality there are very few speculators that even trade the proposed new limit of 200 contracts and that therefore this could not be a justification for the decline. September lost 4.70 cents/lb to close at 117.15 cents/lb, while December closed 4.40 cents lower at 106.90 cents/lb. The back months lost between 3.25 to 4.25 cents/lb.

UNITED STATES - The Coffee, Cocoa and Sugar Exchange's board of managers voted to reduce the speculative position limit from 500 to 200 contracts for any month for which delivery notices have been or may be issued. It is expected that they will be effective beginning with December 1996.

COLOMBIA - Colombia's main coffee harvest is not only expected to be a poor one but it will come in later than usual this year, industry sources told Reuters. This could affect prices as the market is already suffering from tight supply. Foreign Trade Minister Morris Harf said earlier in September that Colombia would be forced to draw on internal stocks maintained by the National Coffee Growers Federation to meet its export commitments this year. He added Colombia would export a total of 10.6 million 60-kg bags in 1996, including 5.15 million bags between July and December. Colombia normally retains about 1 million 60-kg bags from a given year's crop to meet domestic demand and replenish inventories. The National Coffee Growers Federation has estimated total production for calendar year 1996 at 10.5 million bags, down from 12.5 million bags in 1995. Farmers said that in addition to adverse weather the 1996 crop has been hurt by soaring production costs, including those associated with fighting the berry borer.

CANADA - Canada imported 236,581 bags of coffee in March 1996, 14 percent more than was imported the same month the previous year. That brought total imports since the beginning of 1996 up to 660,300 bags, 15 percent more than was imported the same period in 1995. Total imports in calendar year 1995 dropped sharply by 11 percent to 2.510 million bags. Major suppliers of green coffee in January/March 1996 were Guatemala (73,000 vs 56,800 bags), Mexico (67,700 vs 29,100 bags) and Colombia (124,000 vs 85,200 bags). The country exported 66,800 bags of coffee in January/March 1996, 31 percent less than was exported the same period in 1995. Total exports in calendar year 1995 dropped by 9.2 percent to 303,800 bags.
